mainTopic: How דוד המלך prepared for war (אחיתופל, the סנהדרין, the אורים ותומים, then יואב); the פסוק showing that דוד's כינור woke him at midnight; and רבי זירא's new answer about whether משה and דוד knew the exact moment of חצות
overview: This amud finishes a דרשה about how דוד prepared for war. First he took advice from אחיתופל, then from the סנהדרין under בניהו, then he asked the אורים ותומים through אביתר. Only after all that was יואב sent out with the army. The גמרא then gives the פסוק showing that דוד's כינור woke him at midnight. It also brings two answers to why משה said "כחצות." רבי זירא says משה knew the exact time but spoke carefully so that פרעה's astrologers would not call him a liar. רב אשי says כחצות means "at a midnight like this one right now." Next, לוי and רבי יצחק explain why דוד called himself a חסיד: either he rose at חצות, or he humbly did messy work in הלכה and let his teacher מפיבשת check his rulings, which led to the story of his wise son כלאב. The גמרא asks how דוד could call himself a חסיד when he doubted his reward, and answers that he feared a future sin (שמא יגרום החטא), backing this up with יעקב and with the missing miracle in עזרא's time. Finally, it returns to the משנה and asks whose reading of 'בשכבך' the חכמים follow when they say "until midnight." That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: בניהו stands for the סנהדרין and אביתר for the אורים ותומים
steps.stepSummary: The דרשה continues. It explains two more names in the פסוק: בניהו בן יהוידע means the סנהדרין, and אביתר means the אורים ותומים.
steps.simpleTranslation: "בניהו בן יהוידע": this means the סנהדרין. "And אביתר": this means the אורים ותומים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps going through the names in the פסוק about דוד's war plans. It tells us what each of the next two names stands for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each name stands for a stage that the plan had to pass. After אחיתופל gave advice, the plan went to the סנהדרין, headed by בניהו. Then it went to the אורים ותומים, which אביתר the כהן was in charge of asking.

keyTerms.meaning: The great court of Torah judges
The holy names placed inside the breastplate of the כהן גדול, used to ask ה׳ questions
A leader in דוד's time; here, the head of the סנהדרין
The כהן who was in charge of asking the אורים ותומים

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. It is the middle of a דרשה that started on the previous עמוד, where אחיתופל was already explained as דוד's adviser.

phrases.english: "Benayahu ben Yehoyada": this is the Sanhedrin,
phrases.notes: He was the head of the סנהדרין.

phrases.english: "and Evyatar": these are the Urim VeTummim.
phrases.notes: אביתר the כהן asked the אורים ותומים questions (שמואל א כג:ט).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the דרשה from the previous עמוד, after אחיתופל was explained as the adviser.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the פסוק's order, בניהו בן יהוידע stands for the סנהדרין, and אביתר stands for the אורים ותומים.

steps.title: A verse proves בניהו headed the סנהדרין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק from שמואל ב showing that בניהו was in charge of the כרתי and פלתי. This is a name for the סנהדרין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: "And בניהו בן יהוידע was over the כרתי and over the פלתי."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that בניהו really was the head of the סנהדרין. It quotes a פסוק saying he was in charge of the כרתי and פלתי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 just said that בניהו means the סנהדרין. This פסוק backs that up by putting בניהו over a group called כרתי ופלתי. The next steps will show that this group is the סנהדרין.

keyTerms.meaning: "And so it says": introduces a supporting פסוק
A group that בניהו was in charge of; here understood as the סנהדרין

phrases.english: And so it says:
"And Benayahu ben Yehoyada
was over the Kereti and over the Peleti."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב כ:כג

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק to support the claim in step 1 that בניהו stands for the סנהדרין.
steps.raayaObject: That בניהו בן יהוידע was the head of the סנהדרין
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל ב כ:כג: "ובניהו בן יהוידע על הכרתי ועל הפלתי"

steps.title: Why are they called כרתי and פלתי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the סנהדרין is called by the names כרתי and פלתי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why were they called "כרתי" and "פלתי"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the strange names כרתי and פלתי mean. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in step 2 only works if כרתי ופלתי really is the סנהדרין. Explaining the names shows why they fit a court of wise judges. This is a real question asking for an explanation, not an attack.

keyTerms.meaning: "And why were they called...?": asks the reason for a name

phrases.english: And why were they called by the name
"Kereti" and "Peleti"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the names used in the פסוק quoted in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning behind the names כרתי and פלתי, which shows they describe the סנהדרין

steps.title: The names describe decisive and wondrous rulings
steps.stepSummary: כרתי comes from כורתים, because they decided matters clearly. פלתי comes from מופלאים, because their words were wondrous.
steps.simpleTranslation: "כרתי": because they cut (decided) their words clearly. "פלתי": because they were wondrous in their words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Each name is read as a play on words that describes the judges of the סנהדרין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כרתי sounds like כורת, "to cut," meaning their rulings were sharp and final. פלתי sounds like פלא, "wonder," meaning their wisdom was amazing. Both describe a great court, so the proof that בניהו headed the סנהדרין holds up.

keyTerms.meaning: They "cut" their words: their rulings were decisive and final
They were wondrous in their words: their wisdom was amazing

phrases.english: "Kereti": because they cut (decided) their words,
phrases.notes: From the root כרת, to cut.

phrases.english: "Peleti": because they were wondrous in their words.
phrases.notes: From the root פלא, wonder.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: כרתי means they were decisive in their rulings, and פלתי means their words were wondrous. These are qualities of the סנהדרין.

steps.title: Only afterward was יואב the general sent out
steps.stepSummary: The דרשה ends. Only after the adviser, the סנהדרין, and the אורים ותומים had all approved did יואב, the head of the army, get the order to go to war.
steps.simpleTranslation: And only afterward: "the general of the king's army, יואב."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes going through the פסוק. The army is sent out last, only after all the earlier steps were done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order of names in the פסוק teaches the order of steps before a war. First came אחיתופל's advice, then the סנהדרין, then the אורים ותומים, and only then יואב and the army. The military step came only after wisdom, Torah law, and ה׳'s answer had all been checked.

keyTerms.meaning: And only afterward
The general, head of the army
דוד's army general

steps.whatToRemember: דוד's process for going to war followed the order in the פסוק: (1) אחיתופל for advice, (2) בניהו and the סנהדרין, (3) אביתר and the אורים ותומים, (4) only then יואב and the army.

phrases.english: And afterward
"the general of the king's army, Yoav."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א כז:לד

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַחַר כָּךְ שַׂר צָבָא לַמֶּלֶךְ יוֹאָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reading of the פסוק that steps 1–4 were explaining.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The army under יואב was sent out only after advice, the סנהדרין, and the אורים ותומים had all been consulted in order.

steps.title: The verse showing דוד's כינור woke him
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק (בר אדא, or בריה דרב אידי) brings the פסוק that shows דוד's כינור woke him at midnight: "עורה כבודי, עורה הנבל וכנור, אעירה שחר."
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר אדא said, and some say רב יצחק בריה דרב אידי said: What is the verse? "Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will wake the dawn."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to an earlier topic: the כינור that hung above דוד's bed and played by itself at midnight. Now it gives the פסוק that teaches this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא said the north wind blew on the כינור at midnight and woke דוד. Here the source is given. The harp and lyre are already "awake" (playing), and דוד then says "I will wake the dawn," meaning he learns Torah until morning.

keyTerms.meaning: "And some say": the same teaching is said in the name of a different speaker
"What is the verse?": asks for the פסוק that is the source
Harp and lyre
"I will wake the dawn": I am up before the dawn

steps.confusionAlert: "מאי קרא" here is not a challenge. It simply asks which פסוק is the source for the story of the כינור told earlier on עמוד ב.

phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Adda said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: and some say Rav Yitzchak the son of Rav Idi said:
What is the verse?
phrases.notes: The source that the כינור woke דוד at midnight.

phrases.english: "Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre;
I will wake the dawn."
phrases.notes: תהלים נז:ט

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the war דרשה and goes back to the earlier story (עמוד ב) about the כינור over דוד's bed.
steps.raayaObject: That דוד's כינור played by itself and woke him at midnight
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים נז:ט: "עורה כבודי עורה הנבל וכנור אעירה שחר"

steps.title: רבי זירא says both משה and דוד knew the exact time
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא gives a new answer to the sugya's question. Both משה and דוד knew exactly when חצות was.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: משה certainly knew, and דוד also knew.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא opens a new way to answer the earlier question. משה said "כחצות" (about midnight), while דוד knew "חצות לילה" exactly, so did משה not know the exact time? רבי זירא says they both knew, and his explanation for why משה said "כחצות" anyway comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier answers suggested that someone was unsure of the exact moment of midnight. רבי זירא rejects that idea and says both knew precisely. This sets up the next question: if משה knew, why did he say "about midnight"? Steps 10–11 ask and answer this.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: really, certainly
He knew
Also
Midnight

steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the direction of the sugya. The question is no longer whether משה or דוד knew the exact time, but why משה chose the word "כחצות."

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
Moshe certainly knew,
phrases.notes: He knew the exact moment of midnight.

phrases.english: and David also knew.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לְעוֹלָם הֲוָה יָדַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the main question of the sugya (משה's "כחצות" versus דוד's "חצות לילה") and offers a new approach. The challenges to it and their answers follow right away in steps 8–12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both משה and דוד knew the exact moment of חצות.

steps.title: If דוד knew the time, why did he need a כינור?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי זירא's claim that דוד knew exactly when חצות was. If he knew, the כינור seems pointless.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since דוד knew when midnight was, why did he need a lyre?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי זירא's answer. If דוד already knew when חצות was, the story of the כינור waking him seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the כינור was presented as the way דוד knew the time. רבי זירא said דוד knew the time anyway. So the גמרא asks what job the כינור still had.

keyTerms.meaning: Lyre or harp. It hung over דוד's bed.
He knew
Why does he need it? What is it for?

phrases.english: And since David knew (when midnight was),
why did he need a lyre?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵיוָן דְּדָוִד הֲוָה יָדַע, כִּנּוֹר לְמָה לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in step 7 that דוד knew the time, using the כינור from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's claim that דוד knew exactly when חצות was
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If דוד knew the time on his own, the כינור that woke him at midnight had no purpose.

steps.title: The lyre was only there to wake him up
steps.stepSummary: דוד knew when חצות was. He needed the כינור only to wake up from sleep at that moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was to wake him from his sleep.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the כינור did not tell דוד the time. It was his alarm clock to get him out of bed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing the time and waking up at that time are two different things. דוד knew when חצות was, but a sleeping person still needs something to wake him. The כינור did that job.

keyTerms.meaning: To wake up, to be roused
His sleep

phrases.english: To wake him from his sleep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the כינור's function: it was for waking, not for knowing the time.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The כינור was how דוד knew when midnight came.
steps.terutzMaskana: דוד knew the time. The כינור only woke him.

steps.title: If משה knew the time, why did he say 'about midnight'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that משה knew exactly when חצות was. If he did, why did he use the vague word כחצות?
steps.simpleTranslation: And since משה knew when midnight was, why did he need to say 'about midnight'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same kind of question about משה. If משה knew the exact moment of חצות, why did he speak loosely?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word כחצות sounds like 'around midnight,' an estimate. Someone who knows the exact time should just say 'at midnight' (בחצות). So משה's wording seems to clash with רבי זירא's claim.

keyTerms.meaning: About midnight, or 'like midnight'
To say

phrases.english: And since Moses knew (when midnight was),
why did he need to say 'about midnight'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵיוָן דְּמֹשֶׁה הֲוָה יָדַע, לְמָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר כַּחֲצוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel challenge to step 8, now aimed at משה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's claim that משה knew exactly when חצות was
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who knows the exact time would not use the vague word כחצות.

steps.title: משה was worried פרעה's astrologers would miscalculate
steps.stepSummary: משה knew the exact time. He spoke vaguely so that פרעה's astrologers, who might count wrong, would not call him a liar.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה thought: perhaps פרעה's astrologers will make a mistake about the time, and they will say, 'משה is a liar.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that משה used the vague word on purpose. The problem was not his own knowledge but how others might misjudge it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If משה had said 'exactly at midnight' and the Egyptian astrologers wrongly thought midnight came earlier, they would see nothing happen at 'their' midnight. They would then call משה a fake. Saying 'about midnight' protected him from a false accusation.

keyTerms.meaning: He held, he thought
Astrologers
Liar, fabricator

phrases.english: Moses thought:
perhaps Pharaoh's astrologers will err (about the time),
and they will say, 'Moses is a liar.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה קָסָבַר: שֶׁמָּא יִטְעוּ אִצְטַגְנִינֵי פַּרְעֹה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The vague wording was chosen for the listeners' sake, not because משה lacked knowledge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כחצות shows that משה did not know the exact time.
steps.terutzMaskana: משה knew the time. He spoke vaguely so others' errors would not make him look like a liar.

steps.title: Support: train yourself to say 'I don't know'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up משה's caution with a known teaching: get used to saying 'I don't know' so you won't be caught looking like a liar.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Master said: Teach your tongue to say 'I do not know,' or you may be made out to be a liar and be caught.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a general teaching to support the answer about משה. It shows that משה acted on a known principle of careful speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching says not to claim more certainty than is safe, because one mistake can make you look dishonest. משה's word כחצות follows this advice. The teaching gives his choice a solid basis.

keyTerms.meaning: As the Master said (quoting an earlier teaching)
I do not know
You will be shown to be a liar and be caught

steps.whatToRemember: משה knew the exact time of חצות. He said כחצות only so that others' miscalculations would not make him look false.

phrases.english: As the Master said:
Teach your tongue to say 'I do not know,'
lest you be made out a liar and be caught.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר מָר: לַמֵּד לְשׁוֹנְךָ לוֹמַר אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer given in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: משה's choice to say כחצות out of caution
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching of מר: 'Teach your tongue to say I do not know'

steps.title: רב אשי: כחצות means like this midnight right now
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer. משה spoke at midnight between the 13th and 14th of ניסן. כחצות means 'tomorrow at a time like this midnight now,' not 'about midnight.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: משה was standing at midnight of the 13th, going into the 14th. This is what משה told ישראל: הקדוש ברוך הוא said, 'Tomorrow, at a midnight like right now, I will go out into the midst of מצרים.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers another way to solve the question about משה. He says the word כחצות never meant 'about.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב אשי's reading, the letter כ means 'like,' a comparison, not an estimate. משה was speaking at midnight itself and said that tomorrow's plague would come at the same time as this very moment. So there is no vagueness to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: The middle of the night, midnight
Of the 13th going into the 14th (of ניסן)
Like right now, like this moment

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read כחצות here as 'approximately midnight.' For רב אשי, the כ means 'like': tomorrow's midnight will be like tonight's midnight, which is happening as משה speaks.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer removes the question entirely instead of explaining it away. It also confirms that משה knew the exact moment of חצות.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
At midnight of the thirteenth
going into the fourteenth, he (Moses) was standing,
and this is what Moses said to Israel:
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
Tomorrow, at a midnight like this one right now,
I will go out into the midst of Egypt.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: בְּפַלְגָא אוּרְתָּא דִתְלֵיסַר נָגְהֵי אַרְבֵּסַר הֲוָה קָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternative to רבי זירא's approach (step 7): instead of explaining why משה chose a vague word, רב אשי reads כחצות as a comparison, so the question about the wording (step 10) never comes up.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the word: the כ in כחצות is a comparison, not an estimate.
steps.terutzMaskana: כחצות means 'at a midnight like this one,' so משה spoke with full precision.

steps.title: דוד's חסידות: he rose at חצות while other kings slept late
steps.stepSummary: A new topic opens with the פסוק 'שמרה נפשי כי חסיד אני'. לוי and רבי יצחק discuss it. The first view says דוד called himself a חסיד because he got up at חצות to praise ה', while other kings slept until three hours into the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Of דוד... Guard my soul, for I am pious.' לוי and רבי יצחק discussed this. One said: This is what דוד said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: 'Master of the world, am I not pious? All the kings of the East and the West sleep until three hours into the day, but I rise at midnight to give thanks to You.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new teaching about דוד, sparked by the midnight theme. It quotes a פסוק, names the two אמוראים who discuss it, and gives the first opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד calls himself a חסיד, which means someone who goes beyond what is required. The first opinion explains what he meant: a king could easily sleep late like all other kings, yet דוד got up at חצות to thank ה'. That extra effort is what made him a חסיד.

keyTerms.meaning: A pious person who goes beyond what is required
One (of them) said
Master of the world
To give thanks

steps.confusionAlert: 'חד אמר' means 'one of them said.' The גמרא does not tell us whether this is לוי or רבי יצחק. The other opinion comes in step 15.

phrases.english: 'Of David... Guard my soul, for I am pious.'
Levi and Rabbi Yitzchak (discussed this).
One said:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אָמַר דָּוִד לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: This is what David said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:

phrases.aramaic: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, לֹא חָסִיד אֲנִי?
phrases.english: Master of the world, am I not pious?
For all the kings of the East and the West
sleep until three hours (into the day),
but I, 'At midnight I rise to give thanks to You.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לְדָוִד, שָׁמְרָה נַפְשִׁי כִּי חָסִיד אָנִי. לֵוִי וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק. חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the question of how דוד knew חצות to a new דרשה praising his rising at חצות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד called himself a חסיד because, unlike other kings who slept late, he rose at חצות to praise ה'.

steps.title: Second view: דוד dirtied his hands to help women become permitted to their husbands
steps.stepSummary: The other opinion explains דוד's claim to be a חסיד differently. Other kings sat in honor, while דוד personally examined blood, a miscarried fetus, and afterbirth to rule a woman טהור for her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other Sage said: This is what דוד said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the World, am I not a חסיד? All the kings of the East and the West sit in groups enjoying their honor. But my hands get dirty with blood, a miscarried fetus, and afterbirth, so that I can declare a woman pure for her husband.
steps.whatsHappening: In Step 14, one Sage said דוד was a חסיד because he got up at חצות. Now the other Sage gives a different reason: דוד did messy, humble work to help married couples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is the contrast between דוד and other kings. They used their status to enjoy honor. דוד put royal dignity aside and handled unpleasant cases of טומאה himself, all to help a woman become permitted to her husband.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the second Sage in the מחלוקת)
In groups, in groups (sitting together in royal circles)
A miscarried fetus at an early stage
Placenta or afterbirth
To declare a woman pure so she is permitted to her husband

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. It is the second side of the disagreement between לוי and רבי יצחק from Step 14 about the פסוק 'שמרה נפשי כי חסיד אני'.

phrases.english: And the other [Sage said]: This is what David said
phrases.notes: Introduces the second opinion from Step 14.

phrases.english: before the Holy One, Blessed be He:

phrases.aramaic: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, לֹא חָסִיד אֲנִי?
phrases.english: Master of the World, am I not pious?
phrases.notes: This is the claim from the פסוק 'כי חסיד אני'.

phrases.english: For all the kings of the East and the West
sit in groups and groups in their honor,
but as for me, my hands are soiled with blood
phrases.notes: He examines blood to decide whether it makes a woman a נדה.

phrases.english: and with a miscarried fetus and with afterbirth
in order to declare a woman pure for her husband.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, כָּךְ אָמַר דָּוִד לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second Sage's explanation of 'כי חסיד אני', as an alternative to getting up at חצות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד was a חסיד because, unlike other kings who sat in honor, he personally dealt with questions of טומאה to permit wives to their husbands.

steps.title: דוד asked his teacher מפיבשת to check every ruling without shame
steps.stepSummary: דוד adds a second proof of his humility. He checked every ruling with his teacher מפיבשת and was not embarrassed to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: And more than that: in everything I do, I consult my teacher מפיבשת. I say to him: מפיבשת my teacher, did I judge correctly? Did I find someone guilty correctly? Did I find someone innocent correctly? Did I declare something pure correctly? Did I declare something impure correctly? And I was not embarrassed.
steps.whatsHappening: דוד continues the same speech. He adds that even though he is king, he asks his teacher to check all his rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes one level past the dirty work in Step 15. A king letting someone else review and correct his decisions is a big drop in royal honor. דוד is proud that he was not ashamed to do it.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but also
Consults, asks advice
דוד's teacher, from the family of שאול
I found guilty / I found innocent
And I was not ashamed

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא כָּל מָה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה,
phrases.english: And not only that, but in everything that I do,
I consult with Mefivoshet my teacher,
and I say to him: 'Mefivoshet my teacher, did I judge properly?
Did I convict properly? Did I acquit properly?
phrases.notes: These are court rulings in money and judgment cases.

phrases.english: Did I declare pure properly? Did I declare impure properly?'
phrases.notes: These are rulings on טומאה and טהרה.

phrases.english: And I was not ashamed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא כָּל מָה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second proof of דוד's humility to the same speech.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד submitted all his rulings to his teacher's review and was not ashamed to do it.
steps.whatToRemember: In the second view, דוד's חסידות means humility. He gave up royal honor both to do messy work for others and to have his rulings checked.

steps.title: A verse that hints to דוד speaking Torah before kings without shame
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בריה דרב אידי finds a פסוק in תהלים that matches דוד's words 'ולא בושתי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בריה דרב אידי said: What פסוק teaches this? 'I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports דוד's statement with a פסוק. דוד himself wrote in תהלים that he spoke Torah before kings and was not ashamed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'ולא אבוש' match 'ולא בושתי' from Step 16. 'Before kings' can mean in contrast to the other kings, or in front of מפיבשת, who came from a royal family. Either way, the פסוק shows that דוד's lack of shame about Torah was something he said himself.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the verse? (asks for a source in תנ״ך)
Your testimonies, meaning ה׳'s laws
And I will not be ashamed

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rav Idi said:
What is the verse [that hints to this]?
'And I will speak of Your testimonies before kings
phrases.notes: תהלים קי״ט:מ״ו

phrases.english: and I will not be ashamed.'
phrases.notes: Matches דוד's words 'ולא בושתי'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a scriptural hint for דוד's claim that he was not ashamed.
steps.raayaObject: דוד's statement that he consulted מפיבשת and was not ashamed.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים קי״ט:מ״ו: 'ואדברה בעדתיך נגד מלכים ולא אבוש'.

steps.title: Why he was called מפיבשת, and דוד's reward of a wise son
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that his real name was איש בשת. He was called מפיבשת because he embarrassed דוד in הלכה, and because דוד accepted this humbly, he merited a son named כלאב.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא taught: His name was not מפיבשת. His name was איש בשת. Why was he called מפיבשת? Because he would embarrass דוד in הלכה. Because of this, דוד merited that כלאב came from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains the name מפיבשת. It also says דוד was rewarded for accepting correction humbly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name is read as a wordplay: מפי־בשת, 'from his mouth came embarrassment', because his corrections shamed דוד. דוד did not resent this. As a reward for that humility, he had a very wise son, כלאב.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (introduces a teaching from the תנאים)
The name the ברייתא says was his real name
Embarrasses
Therefore he merited
A son of דוד known for great wisdom

steps.confusionAlert: In תנ״ך, מפיבשת is יונתן's son and איש בשת is שאול's son. The ברייתא is not mixing up the people. It is making a point through the names: the 'בשת' (shame) in his name came from the way he embarrassed דוד in הלכה.

phrases.english: It was taught: His name was not 'Mefivoshet',
rather, 'Ish Boshet' was his name,
So why was he called Mefivoshet?
Because he would embarrass David's face in matters of halacha,
phrases.notes: Wordplay: מפי־בשת, 'from his mouth, shame'.

phrases.english: therefore David merited
that Kilav came out from him.
phrases.notes: כלאב was a son of דוד, known for great wisdom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the name of the teacher mentioned in Step 16 and adds דוד's reward for his humility.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name מפיבשת reflects that he embarrassed דוד in הלכה. דוד's humble acceptance earned him a wise son, כלאב.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that being willing to be corrected in Torah is rewarded, and the reward is fitting: a son who would himself be great in Torah.

steps.title: כלאב's real name was דניאל, and why he was called כלאב
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says כלאב's real name was דניאל. He was called כלאב because he would embarrass מפיבשת in הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: His name was not כלאב. His name was דניאל. Why was he called כלאב? Because he would embarrass מפיבשת in הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן explains the name כלאב the same way the ברייתא explained מפיבשת. The name comes from embarrassing someone in הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name כלאב is read as a wordplay: מכלים אב, 'he shames the father/teacher', meaning מפיבשת, דוד's teacher. This completes the circle. The one who embarrassed דוד was later outdone by דוד's own son, so דוד's humility was repaid.

keyTerms.meaning: The name of דוד's son as it appears in another list in תנ״ך
Embarrasses, puts to shame

steps.whatToRemember: The names tell the story. מפיבשת embarrassed דוד in הלכה, דוד accepted it humbly, and as a reward his son כלאב (מכלים אב) outdid מפיבשת in הלכה.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said: His name was not 'Kilav',
rather, 'Daniel' was his name,
phrases.notes: In דברי הימים א׳ ג׳:א׳, דוד's son is called דניאל.

phrases.english: So why was he called 'Kilav'?
Because he would embarrass Mefivoshet's face in matters of halacha.
phrases.notes: Wordplay: כלאב = מכלים אב, 'shames the teacher'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the name כלאב from Step 18 in the same pattern as the explanation of מפיבשת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כלאב's real name was דניאל. He was called כלאב because he embarrassed מפיבשת in הלכה.

steps.title: שלמה's verses about the wise son כלאב
steps.stepSummary: שלמה's words in משלי are read as describing דוד's joy over his wise son כלאב.
steps.simpleTranslation: About him (כלאב), שלמה said in his wisdom: 'My son, if your heart is wise, my heart will be glad, even mine.' And it also says: 'Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, so that I can answer those who taunt me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two פסוקים from משלי to show how happy דוד was that his son כלאב became so wise. This closes the story of כלאב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second פסוק fits the story especially well. 'So that I can answer those who taunt me' matches כלאב being able to answer מפיבשת in הלכה. דוד was humble when he was corrected, and his reward was a son who could hold his own in Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: שלמה in his wisdom, meaning his book משלי
'and it says': introduces a second supporting פסוק
those who taunt or shame me
so that I may answer back

steps.whatToRemember: The כלאב story ends here. דוד's humility before מפיבשת was rewarded with a son wise enough to answer מפיבשת himself.

phrases.english: And about him Solomon said in his wisdom:
phrases.notes: 'Him' refers to כלאב, from the previous step.

phrases.english: 'My son, if your heart is wise,'
phrases.notes: משלי 23:15

phrases.english: 'my heart will be glad, even mine.'
And it says: 'Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad,'
phrases.notes: משלי 27:11

phrases.english: 'so that I may answer those who taunt me.'
phrases.notes: This matches כלאב answering מפיבשת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the story of כלאב from step 19 with פסוקים.
steps.raayaObject: דוד's joy at his son כלאב's wisdom in הלכה

steps.title: Would דוד really call himself a חסיד?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges דוד's claim 'כי חסיד אני' from the dotted word לולא, which shows דוד was unsure of his share in the World to Come.
steps.simpleTranslation: Would דוד call himself a חסיד? But it is written: 'If I had not believed I would see the goodness of ה׳ in the land of the living.' And it was taught in the name of רבי יוסי: Why are there dots over the word 'לולא'? דוד said before הקב״ה: Master of the World, I am sure that You give good reward to the צדיקים in the future, but I do not know if I have a share among them or not!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the opening פסוק, 'שמרה נפשי כי חסיד אני.' It asks how דוד could call himself a חסיד when another פסוק shows he was unsure he deserved a reward at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dots over a word in the written text of תנ״ך signal doubt or reservation. רבי יוסי reads the dots on לולא (in תהלים) as דוד admitting he did not know whether he would be counted among the צדיקים. That seems to contradict דוד confidently calling himself a חסיד.

keyTerms.meaning: Does he call himself...? (a challenging question)
But is it not written...? (introduces a contradicting פסוק)
'If not': a word in תהלים 27:13 that has dots over it
dotted: marked with dots above the letters
in the future, meaning the World to Come

steps.confusionAlert: The dots are not vowels. They are special marks placed above certain words in the written text, and חז״ל read them as hinting at doubt.

phrases.english: And does David call himself 'pious'?
phrases.notes: Refers back to 'כי חסיד אני' (תהלים 86:2).

phrases.english: But isn't it written: 'If I had not believed'
phrases.notes: תהלים 27:13

phrases.english: 'to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living,'
and it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
Why are there dots over 'לולא'?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר דָּוִד לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: David said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the World,
I am confident in You
that You pay good reward to the righteous
in the World to Come,
but I do not know
whether I have a share among them
or not?!
phrases.notes: This doubt seems to contradict calling himself a חסיד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the כלאב story and returns to challenge דוד's claim of being a חסיד.
steps.kashyaTarget: דוד's statement 'שמרה נפשי כי חסיד אני'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone confident that he is a חסיד would not doubt his share in the reward of the צדיקים. Yet the dotted לולא shows that דוד did doubt it.

steps.title: דוד feared a future sin
steps.stepSummary: דוד knew he was a צדיק. His only worry was that a sin might cause him to lose his reward.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps a sin will cause it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question in just a few words. דוד's doubt was not about his present righteousness. He was afraid that a sin might cost him his reward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two פסוקים are talking about different things. 'כי חסיד אני' describes who דוד is right now. 'לולא' expresses fear of what a sin could do to him. So both פסוקים can be true together.

keyTerms.meaning: perhaps a sin will cause (the loss of the promise or reward)

phrases.english: Perhaps the sin will cause it.
phrases.notes: The reward is guaranteed only as long as one does not sin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: present righteousness versus fear of a future sin
steps.terutzHavaAmina: דוד's doubt meant he did not think he was righteous.
steps.terutzMaskana: דוד knew he was a חסיד, but he feared that a sin could cause him to lose his reward.

steps.title: יעקב also feared that sin might cancel a promise
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב בר אידי points to a contradiction: הקב״ה promised to protect יעקב, yet יעקב was very afraid. The answer is the same idea, that he feared a sin might cancel the promise.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like רבי יעקב בר אידי's teaching, for רבי יעקב בר אידי pointed out a contradiction. It is written: 'Behold, I am with you and I will guard you wherever you go,' and it is written: 'And יעקב was very afraid.' He said: יעקב was afraid that perhaps a sin would cause the promise to be lost.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the answer from step 22 with a parallel case about יעקב אבינו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הקב״ה gave יעקב a direct promise of protection, yet יעקב was terrified of עשו. רבי יעקב בר אידי explains that a promise can be lost through sin. This shows that a great צדיק can rightly fear losing what he was promised, which is exactly what we said about דוד.

keyTerms.meaning: he raised a contradiction (between two פסוקים)
and I will guard you
and he was afraid

steps.whatToRemember: A promise or reward from הקב״ה can be lost through sin. So even a צדיק like דוד or יעקב can be sure of who he is now and still fear the future.
steps.whyThisMatters: This idea of שמא יגרום החטא comes up often in the גמרא, and the rest of this sugya continues to build on it.

phrases.english: As in the teaching of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi,
for Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction:
It is written: 'Behold, I am with you'
phrases.notes: בראשית 28:15, the vision of the ladder

phrases.english: 'and I will guard you wherever you go,'
and it is written: 'And Jacob was very afraid'
phrases.notes: בראשית 32:8, before meeting עשו

phrases.english: He said: Perhaps the sin will cause it.
phrases.notes: יעקב feared that a sin he might have committed since the promise would cancel it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידִי, דְּרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידִי רָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel source to support the answer of step 22.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a righteous person may fear that a sin will cancel a promised good
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יעקב בר אידי's resolution of the contradiction between בראשית 28:15 and 32:8

steps.title: A ברייתא quotes a doubled verse from שירת הים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up the idea that sin can cancel a promise. It first quotes the verse, which repeats the phrase 'until [the people] cross over' twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא taught: 'Until Your people cross over, ה׳, until the people You acquired cross over.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing a source to support step 23's idea that sin can undo a promise. This step only quotes the verse and sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse seems to repeat itself, saying 'until they cross over' two times. The ברייתא will treat this repetition as a hint to two different crossings into ארץ ישראל. That reading is what turns the verse into a proof.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה)
Until [they] cross over
The people You acquired

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the two halves of the verse as simple poetic repetition. The whole proof depends on treating them as two separate events.

phrases.english: As it was taught (in a Baraita):
phrases.notes: Introduces a supporting source for step 23.

phrases.english: "Until Your people cross over, O Lord,
phrases.notes: First half of the doubled phrase (שמות 15:16).

phrases.english: until the people You acquired cross over."
phrases.notes: Second half. The repetition is the key to the דרשה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to support step 23's claim that sin can cancel a Divine promise, which is why a צדיק may fear it.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that sin can cause a promise or a deserved miracle to go unfulfilled.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading of שמות 15:16 (שירת הים).

steps.title: Two entries into the Land, and the miracle that sin prevented
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains that the first phrase refers to the entry with יהושע and the second to the return with עזרא. From this the חכמים learn that Israel deserved a miracle in עזרא's time, but sin stopped it.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Until Your people cross over, ה׳' refers to the first entry into the Land. 'Until the people You acquired cross over' refers to the second entry. From here the חכמים said: ישראל deserved to have a miracle done for them in the days of עזרא, the same way one was done for them in the days of יהושע בן נון. But sin caused it not to happen.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the doubled verse as two entries into ארץ ישראל. It concludes that the second entry should have had a miracle too, but sin got in the way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since one verse puts both entries side by side, they should have been equal, with open miracles both times. In עזרא's time there was no such miracle, and the ברייתא says sin was the cause. This is a real-life example of exactly what יעקב and דוד feared: something deserved can be lost through sin.

keyTerms.meaning: The first entry into ארץ ישראל, in the time of יהושע
The second entry, the return from בבל in the time of עזרא
A miracle
That sin caused it [not to happen]

steps.whatToRemember: The side discussion ends with a clear rule: even something promised or deserved can be lost because of sin. That is why יעקב and דוד were afraid, even though they were צדיקים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the whole aggadic tangent from steps 21 to 24 by giving a historical case where sin really did cancel what was deserved.

phrases.english: "Until Your people cross over, O Lord" —
phrases.notes: First half of the verse.

phrases.english: this is the first entry (into the Land),
phrases.notes: The entry with יהושע.

phrases.english: "Until the people You acquired cross over" —
phrases.notes: Second half of the verse.

phrases.english: this is the second entry.
phrases.notes: The return in עזרא's time.

phrases.english: From here the Sages said:
phrases.notes: The lesson drawn from the derasha.

phrases.english: Israel was worthy
of having a miracle done for them in the days of Ezra,
just as one was done for them
in the days of Joshua son of Nun.
phrases.notes: For example, the splitting of the ירדן.

phrases.english: But the sin caused (it not to happen).
phrases.notes: The point of the proof: sin canceled what was deserved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the verse quoted in step 24 and draws the lesson that proves step 23's point.
steps.raayaObject: That sin can cancel a deserved or promised good.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's reading of the two entries into the Land, and the missing miracle in עזרא's time.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Israel deserved a miracle in עזרא's time, like in יהושע's time, but sin prevented it.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: the חכמים say until midnight
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves the aggadic tangent and quotes the next part of the משנה: the חכמים say קריאת שמע at night may be said until חצות.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה says:] 'And the חכמים say: until midnight.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes the view of the חכמים. This is a setup line that prepares the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא analyzed רבי אליעזר's view, which ends at the close of the first watch. Now it turns to the חכמים, who set the deadline at midnight. It quotes their words so it can ask what reasoning stands behind them.

keyTerms.meaning: And the Sages say (the majority view in the משנה)
Until midnight

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. The אגדה about sin is finished, and the גמרא is returning to the משנה's הלכה of when to say קריאת שמע at night.

phrases.english: "And the Sages say: until midnight."
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, brought back for discussion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the aggadic tangent and returns to the משנה's next opinion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the חכמים, the time for קריאת שמע at night lasts until midnight.

steps.title: Whose reading of 'when you lie down' do the חכמים follow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which earlier explanation of 'בשכבך' the חכמים rely on.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion do the חכמים hold?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the חכמים's midnight deadline is based on. This opens a test of the possible options.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The timing of קריאת שמע comes from the word 'בשכבך' ('when you lie down'). Each view understands that word differently. The גמרא wants to know which understanding of 'lying down' would lead to midnight as the deadline.

keyTerms.meaning: Like whom? (whose opinion)
They hold or reason

phrases.english: The Sages — in accordance with whom do they hold?
phrases.notes: Asks for the basis of the midnight deadline.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what reasoning lies behind the משנה line quoted in step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which reading of 'בשכבך' supports the חכמים's deadline of midnight.

steps.title: If they follow רבי אליעזר, they should use his deadline
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests the first option. If the חכמים read 'בשכבך' the way רבי אליעזר does, they should also end at the close of the first watch, as he does.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they hold like רבי אליעזר, then let them say [the deadline] like רבי אליעזר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first possibility and shows that it does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר reads 'בשכבך' as the time when people go to sleep, so he ends at the close of the first watch. If the חכמים shared that reading, they would reach the same deadline, not midnight. Since they say midnight, this option seems wrong, and the גמרא will need another option.

keyTerms.meaning: If
Let them say
The תנא whose deadline is the end of the first watch

phrases.english: If they hold in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer —
phrases.notes: First option tested.

phrases.english: let them say (the same deadline) as Rabbi Eliezer!
phrases.notes: That is, until the end of the first watch, not midnight.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to step 27's question and rejects it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The option that the חכמים share רבי אליעזר's reading of 'בשכבך'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reading of the verse should give the same deadline. The חכמים's different deadline (midnight) shows that they cannot fully share רבי אליעזר's reasoning.
